claims.text: Introducing a small amount of boron into a metallic-glass precursor alloy will enhance its glass-forming ability.
Boron enhances glass-forming ability by inducing local atomic-packing frustration.
Boron-induced atomic-packing frustration suppresses crystallization during rapid quenching.
The parent alloy is prone to crystallization when cooled from its undercooled liquid state.
Boron has an atomic-size mismatch with the atoms of the unspecified parent alloy.
Boron has a negative heat of mixing with the unspecified parent alloy.
Boron's atomic-size mismatch and negative heat of mixing increase atomic-packing disorder and local structural frustration.
Incorporated boron disturbs local atomic order in the liquid alloy.
Boron-induced disruption of local atomic order increases the nucleation energy barrier.
An increased nucleation barrier makes ordered crystalline structures harder to form during cooling.
Boron addition will reduce crystallization relative to the boron-free parent alloy.
Boron addition will produce a higher crystallization-onset temperature in DSC scans than the boron-free baseline.
Boron addition will produce a more pronounced amorphous phase in XRD patterns than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-free parent alloy has limited glass-forming ability because it has relatively low resistance to crystallization during quenching.
The beneficial effect of boron is limited to an optimal concentration range.
Above an unspecified concentration, boron may cause unwanted phase formation.
Above an unspecified concentration, boron may deteriorate other material properties.
